scenes.heading: Container Registries & Image Management
scenes.subheading: Where your images live and how to version them
scenes.narration: A container registry is the central store where you push, pull, and version the images that run your data workloads.

scenes.heading: What a registry does
bullets: Organizes images into repositories and tags
scenes.narration: A registry stores your images and distributes them to any host that needs to run them. It organizes those images into repositories, each holding multiple tagged versions. It enforces access control through authentication so only authorized users can push or pull. And most managed registries scan images for known vulnerabilities before they reach production.

scenes.heading: Tag, push, and pull
scenes.code:
# Build and tag with a version
docker build -t myrepo/pipeline:1.4.0 .

# Log in and push to the registry
docker login registry.example.com
docker push registry.example.com/myrepo/pipeline:1.4.0

# Pull a specific version elsewhere
docker pull registry.example.com/myrepo/pipeline:1.4.0
scenes.narration: First we build the image and tag it with a meaningful semantic version rather than relying on latest. After authenticating to the registry, we push that tagged image so it becomes available to the team. On any other machine, a pull retrieves exactly that version, guaranteeing everyone runs identical code.

scenes.heading: The latest tag trap
scenes.narration: Relying on the latest tag is dangerous because it points to a moving target, making deployments non-reproducible and rollbacks painful. Pinning to an explicit, immutable version tag ensures every environment runs the same image and lets you roll back cleanly to any prior release.

scenes.text: Treat images as versioned artifacts: tag deliberately, scan for vulnerabilities, and never deploy :latest to production.
scenes.narration: Treat every image as a versioned artifact by tagging deliberately, scanning for vulnerabilities, and keeping the latest tag far away from production.
